title: Alternatives in regular expressions should be grouped when used with anchors
description: When using anchors (such as ^ or $) in regular expressions, alternatives (expressions separated by the | operator) should be grouped using parentheses. Without grouping, the anchors may not apply as intended, leading to unexpected matches or bugs. Grouping ensures that the anchor applies to the entire alternation, not just the first or last alternative.
message: Alternatives in regular expressions should be grouped with parentheses when used with anchors to avoid unexpected matches.
impact: If alternatives are not grouped with anchors, the regular expression may match unintended strings, potentially causing logic errors or security vulnerabilities.
recommendation: Always group alternatives with parentheses when using anchors in regular expressions. For example, use ^(foo|bar)$ instead of ^foo|bar$.

noncompliant.description: This pattern matches 'foo' at the start of a string or 'bar' at the end, not both. The anchor does not apply to both alternatives as intended.

compliant.description: This pattern matches either 'foo' or 'bar' as the entire string, as the anchors apply to the grouped alternatives.

devsecops.security: Potential for logic errors or security issues if regular expressions do not match as intended.
devsecops.automation: Helps automated tools detect and prevent regex mistakes.
devsecops.compliance: Not directly related to compliance standards.

why_is_this_an_issue: Without grouping, anchors in regular expressions may not apply to all alternatives, leading to incorrect pattern matching and possible bugs or vulnerabilities.
how_to_fix: Wrap alternatives in parentheses when using anchors in regular expressions. For example, change ^foo|bar$ to ^(foo|bar)$.
